_note: Decision X-008 (docs/audit/DECISIONS.md): after a key choice, two characters who disagree each give a strong reply. Neither reply is marked as the better one. Each entry shows once, after its condition first becomes true.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on your new label

replies.speaker: curator-dace
replies.text: A careful label is the whole job. Visitors read one line and walk on. If that line matches what we can show, the hall is honest.

replies.speaker: clerk-venn
replies.text: A careful label is a start, not the job. Who decided which kind of 'first' gets a line at all? The label answers our question. A visitor may have brought a different one.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the test billet

replies.speaker: smith-hesper
replies.text: You made the pattern yourself in one afternoon. That is the evidence. A pattern on the surface does not prove age, and now you have seen why with your own hands.

replies.speaker: merchant-corvan
replies.text: One billet in one forge proves that the pattern can be new. It does not prove that mine is new. You tested what is possible. You did not test my blade.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on Corvan's new sign

replies.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
replies.text: He changed the sign and kept his stall. That is how a market learns. Shame teaches people to hide. A fair second chance teaches them to check.

replies.speaker: smith-hesper
replies.text: He changed it because a crowd watched. Next month there is no crowd. I want the guild to check the signs, not wait for a Guardian.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the empty signboard

replies.speaker: merchant-corvan
replies.text: No sign is safer than a sign someone can argue with. I have a family to feed. Now buyers will ask me, and I will say less.

replies.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
replies.text: An empty board tells buyers nothing. A true sign would have been worth more to him and to them. Silence is not the same as honesty.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the maker's note

replies.speaker: guildmaster-orrin
replies.text: The old word stays, and the note under it tells the truth. Buyers who read get both. That is a fair market.

replies.speaker: smith-hesper
replies.text: Most buyers read the big word and not the small note. A sign is judged by what people take from it, not by what it says somewhere at the bottom.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the well plan

replies.speaker: well-keeper
replies.text: Two sticks, the same drop, and the whole street heard it together. That was enough to stop the blaming. People needed an answer this week, not next year.

replies.speaker: smith-hesper
replies.text: Two wells on one day is a small check. If the forge is part of the cause, we will not see it until the rains come back. I would keep reading the sticks every week.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the shelf called 'Toys'

replies.speaker: cataloguer-bela
replies.text: A category is a promise about where people will look. Nobody looking for pens looks under 'Toys'. The shelf hid the model.

replies.speaker: curator-dace
replies.text: Every shelf hides something. The clerk filed it by who gave it, and that is worth knowing too. Move the slip, and we hide that instead. A second card can point from one shelf to the other.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the first source

replies.speaker: porter-idris
replies.text: So the record book had it first. Good. Then the story is settled, and I can stop telling the wrong one.

replies.speaker: stallkeeper-hana
replies.text: The book had it first. That tells us where the story started, not whether the book was right. Someone wrote that page, and they heard it from someone too.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the packet for the public case

replies.speaker: nile-nasir
replies.text: The case is where most people look. A crossed-out title shows them that a record can be corrected. That lesson reaches more visitors than any reading table.

replies.speaker: nile-leila
replies.text: A visitor at a case reads two lines and moves on. The workmen's slips need someone to sit down with them. The case teaches that labels change. The table teaches how we know.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the packet for the reading table

replies.speaker: nile-leila
replies.text: The scribe's own words, with his name on them. The readers will hear the workmen first, not the king. That is the right order for this archive.

replies.speaker: nile-nasir
replies.text: The table seats six people. The public case is seen by hundreds, and it still shows the king's boast as fact. A careful packet that few people read leaves the loud claim standing.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the packet for the workshop

replies.speaker: nile-marek
replies.text: Put the trial beside the map and people can test a road with their own hands. A model you can try is worth ten labels you only read.

replies.speaker: nile-iman
replies.text: A model shows what we tried here, today. Some visitors will think the ancient mapmaker tried it too. The card must say clearly where our test ends and the old map begins.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the two records under one name

replies.speaker: nile-leila
replies.text: A name is how people search. If Amunnakht's name leads to both records, a reader finds the man and his work in one step. The limits on each entry keep it honest.

replies.speaker: nile-marek
replies.text: The museum links much of the map's writing to him, not all of it. Put both records under one name and readers will remember the link and forget the 'much of'. Some links should be harder to make.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the copyists' proof

replies.speaker: nile-marek
replies.text: I trust what I can test with my hands. Your arch rests on the word list. Add one word with no vowel, and it falls. A proof is only as strong as the rules under it, and in the world, someone always changes the rules.

replies.speaker: nile-nasir
replies.text: That is exactly why I like it. The arch tells you which stone to watch. A hundred ladders could not tell you that. With a proof, you know what would break it before it breaks.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the two stands

replies.speaker: preserved-royal-keeper
replies.text: Separate stands respect each record. The royal file has its own gap and its own people. Put the two side by side, and visitors read one as the answer to the other.

replies.speaker: preserved-coast-keeper
replies.text: Separate stands are fair, but visitors still compare. They just do it without help, and they bring the old habit of treating a royal tomb as normal and the Chinchorro dead as strange. The Chinchorro were preparing their dead about two thousand years before the earliest Egyptian mummies.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the comparison slip

replies.speaker: preserved-coast-keeper
replies.text: The slip lets visitors see two peoples caring for their dead in different ways, and it asks the question for them. Without it, the coastal stand is just the odd one at the end of the room.

replies.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
replies.text: A slip in the middle makes them a pair, and a pair invites a ranking. At my desk people already ask which was better. The slip has to say what each record can and cannot tell, or it turns into a scoreboard.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on holding the cases

replies.speaker: preserved-registrar
replies.text: Holding the cases is the careful choice. A heading glowed with a mistake once, and it can do it again. The desk lets people ask before we answer for them.

replies.speaker: preserved-inquiry-keeper
replies.text: Careful for us. But the families and the visitors came today. A closed case also says something: that the past is too fragile for them. I would rather open with honest gaps than keep the door shut.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the separate strip

replies.speaker: coast-forecaster
replies.text: A forecast is not a reading, so it gets its own strip with its own condition. When the wind changes, we take down one strip and the measurements stay true.

replies.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
replies.text: Two strips means two things to read, and a cutter at the quay reads one. If they read only the forecast strip, they never see that it rests on the wind. The condition has to be where the eye lands first.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the open space for the next bell

replies.speaker: coast-forecaster
replies.text: An empty space says the honest thing: we will know more at the next bell. People learn to trust a notice that tells them when it will change.

replies.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
replies.text: An empty space also looks like a missing number. Some crews will wait for it and miss the tide. Uncertainty helps only if people know what to do while they wait.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the quay board

replies.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
replies.text: The board stays where everyone can check it again. A notice you can go back to is worth more than one you heard once.

replies.speaker: coast-forecaster
replies.text: The board serves the people who come to the board. The basket crews on the steps never pass it. A careful notice in the wrong place is careful for nobody.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the runner

replies.speaker: coast-forecaster
replies.text: The runner reaches the people with the least time and the most to lose. The steps hear first, and that is the right order.

replies.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
replies.text: A spoken copy changes each time it is passed on. By the third crew, the condition may be gone and only the number left. And when the reading changes, who runs to take the old one back?

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the crews' own words

replies.speaker: forest-steward
replies.text: The crews wrote those notes for each other, in their own words. If we rewrite them into neat lines, we lose who saw what and why they cared. A record of people working should sound like them.

replies.speaker: forest-naturalist
replies.text: Their words are precious, but 'heard wings on the ridge' and 'saw three birds on the ridge' are different kinds of evidence. If the line does not say which is which, a visitor counts a sound as a sighting.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on separate lines for heard and seen

replies.speaker: forest-naturalist
replies.text: A sound and a sighting are different evidence, and now the record shows it. Anyone can count the seen lines and treat the heard ones as leads.

replies.speaker: forest-steward
replies.text: Clean lines, and the crews' voices gone. The lamp crew knows those reeds better than any lookout. Sorting their notes into our columns tells them our way of knowing is the real one.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the quiet creek screen

replies.speaker: forest-steward
replies.text: Small groups at the creek, large groups to the ridge. The birds get their quiet, and the screen stays a place where watching still works.

replies.speaker: forest-naturalist
replies.text: And the people on the bridge who will not climb the ridge? They go home with nothing. A rule that protects the count can also decide who gets to see.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on briefing everyone with both logs

replies.speaker: forest-naturalist
replies.text: Everyone hears both logs and chooses for themselves. That is the fairest thing a record can do: let people decide with the same evidence we had.

replies.speaker: forest-steward
replies.text: Fair to the people, maybe. But if everyone chooses the creek, the creek screen fills, the birds turn away, and tomorrow's log shows a crossing that closed because we watched it.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the window

replies.speaker: metal-inspector
replies.text: The readings in the window are the test, in plain sight. An empty maker clip is honest: the balance cannot tell us who made them, so the clip says nothing.

replies.speaker: metal-steward
replies.text: An empty clip is not silence to a buyer. It looks like a gap someone will fill, and the seller will fill it with a story. The ledger shows where each box went. That is the history the panels actually have.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the movement ledger

replies.speaker: metal-steward
replies.text: The ledger lets a buyer follow each box from the yard, step by step. A claim about origin should rest on the journey, not on how two things look.

replies.speaker: metal-inspector
replies.text: A ledger shows where a box went, not what is in it. Two units against four is the one thing we measured. Hide it behind a long ledger, and most buyers will never reach it.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on one size note

replies.speaker: metal-inspector
replies.text: One size note, two readings under it. The buyer sees at once that the same size did not mean the same weight. That is the surprise, and it should be the first thing they read.

replies.speaker: metal-steward
replies.text: Under one note, the two readings look like one object measured twice. Give each box its own line, or someone will average them and call it a match.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on a reading for each box

replies.speaker: metal-steward
replies.text: Each box keeps its own reading, so nobody can blend them. When the docket turns up, we can follow each box by its letter.

replies.speaker: metal-inspector
replies.text: Two separate cards make two separate stories. The point of the test was the comparison. If the reader has to put the cards side by side themselves, many will not.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the full reprint

replies.speaker: copies-presskeeper
replies.text: A full sheet carries the claim, the trial day and the source together, in one place. Nothing can fall off a sheet that was printed whole.

replies.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
replies.text: A full sheet at the hall door reaches people who already came to the hall. The ones who turned back at the stalls never see it. A complete correction in one place can still leave the wrong copies out there.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the correction strips

replies.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
replies.text: The strips go where the wrong copies already are. That is the only place a correction can catch the people who were misled.

replies.speaker: copies-presskeeper
replies.text: A strip is a small thing pinned to a big one. Strips fall off, and get pinned to the wrong copy. In a year, someone will find the old sheet without its strip and believe it again.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on keeping the sheets in order

replies.speaker: copies-presskeeper
replies.text: In order, the sheets show how the claim changed, one copy at a time. You can point to the exact copy where Tuesday fell out. That is how a press learns.

replies.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
replies.text: A reader at my door does not care which copy changed first. They want to know if the hall is open. The history of the error helps us. The missing time helps them.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on pinning the missing lines

replies.speaker: copies-lendingkeeper
replies.text: The time and the source go back where people read. Whoever picks up a copy now gets what was lost.

replies.speaker: copies-presskeeper
replies.text: Pin the lines back, and the copies look as if they were never wrong. The next printer cannot see where the claim broke, and the same break happens again.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the shore plan first

replies.speaker: sea-harbourkeeper
replies.text: Most people who stop here walk. The shore plan answers their question, and the inset still points the crews to their survey. Put the most used chart where most people look.

replies.speaker: sea-cartographer
replies.text: Most people who stop here walk, and most of them never go near the shoal. The crews do, and a small inset is how a skiff ends up on the shoal. Put the chart that can hurt someone where nobody can miss it.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the shoal chart at full size

replies.speaker: sea-cartographer
replies.text: The shoal chart is short, but it is the one that keeps a boat off the rocks. Full size means a crew can read the depth marks without bending to an inset.

replies.speaker: sea-harbourkeeper
replies.text: And the carriers who asked first get the side wall. They will read the big chart, see water everywhere, and think the shore plan was the small thing it was not. A display also teaches what matters most.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the carriers' names

replies.speaker: sea-harbourkeeper
replies.text: The carriers' names say where work changes hands. Next to the shore plan, those names become a working map, not a list of words.

replies.speaker: sea-cartographer
replies.text: The crew's names come from what they see from the water. Put the carriers' names on the shore plan first, and the market's way of naming the coast becomes the official one, just because it was closer to the desk.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the crew's names

replies.speaker: sea-cartographer
replies.text: A name like 'Lantern House' is a sight point: it tells a crew where to look. Next to the survey, it is a tool, not a label.

replies.speaker: sea-harbourkeeper
replies.text: A tool for the crew. For a carrier, 'Lantern House' is just a building on the wrong side. Every name on a chart says whose way of moving through the place counts first.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the silence first

replies.speaker: stage-director
replies.text: Silence first, and the audience waits with the worker. When the crate moves, they already feel why. The order gives the moment its reason.

replies.speaker: stage-host
replies.text: Silence first, and the audience decides the worker is afraid before anything happens. Half of them will never change that reading. The order does not only give a reason. It chooses one.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the move first

replies.speaker: stage-host
replies.text: The move first lets the audience see what happened before anyone tells them how to feel. Then the silence is theirs to read.

replies.speaker: stage-director
replies.text: Nobody reads a silence fresh. After the crate moves, the pause looks like guilt. You have not left the meaning open. You have picked a darker one.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the front-seat view

replies.speaker: stage-director
replies.text: The front seats see the whole move. That is the staging as we made it. A cast plan should show the scene as it is meant to be seen.

replies.speaker: stage-host
replies.text: As it is meant to be seen by the people with the best seats. The side seats paid too. If the plan shows only the front view, nobody will ever fix what the side cannot see.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the side view

replies.speaker: stage-host
replies.text: The side view shows what most of the hall actually gets: the lines and the rhythm, with the move half hidden. That is the scene the audience really knows.

replies.speaker: stage-director
replies.text: Plan from the worst seat, and you stage for the post, not for the story. Better to fix the post and keep the full move than to shrink the scene to fit it.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on both pairs of readings

replies.speaker: market-assayer
replies.text: Both pairs side by side show the mistake itself: the basket counted as fibre. A buyer who sees how the first tag went wrong can catch the next one.

replies.speaker: market-clerk
replies.text: Four numbers at a busy stall, and the buyer reads the biggest one. Show the net figure first. A household needs to know what it gets, not how the seller got it wrong.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on net figures first

replies.speaker: market-clerk
replies.text: Net first, because fibre is what people pay for. The gross figures still help the carters, so they go where the carters look.

replies.speaker: market-assayer
replies.text: Net first hides the reason the tag was wrong. Next week another seller weighs a heavy basket, and nobody on the queue knows to ask about tare.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on posting the whole-lot line

replies.speaker: market-clerk
replies.text: The whole-lot line tells a buyer with eight credits what they can actually take home today. A cheaper rate they cannot afford is not a real choice.

replies.speaker: market-assayer
replies.text: Today's line is true for today's two lots. Leave it up, and tomorrow someone buys a new crate on a line that was never measured for it.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the reweigh ticket

replies.speaker: market-assayer
replies.text: A reweigh ticket says the honest thing: a new crate gets its own measurement. A quote should never outlive the lot it was weighed on.

replies.speaker: market-clerk
replies.text: Honest, and slow. The first person at the next bell waits at the scale, and the person behind them leaves. Every check has a cost, and the queue pays it.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on seven buckets for the rows

replies.speaker: water-keeper
replies.text: The rows feed the most people for the longest time. Seven there and three below does the most good with ten buckets. Call it a consequences view if you like: I count what each bucket does.

replies.speaker: water-scribe
replies.text: The lower crew agreed to the drought plan on a promise of a fair share. Three is not fair, whatever it grows. I keep to duty here: a promise made in the agreement holds even when breaking it would do more good.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on five and five

replies.speaker: water-scribe
replies.text: An even split keeps the agreement's spirit: both crews carry the drought together, and both can see that they did. People keep a rule they can see is fair.

replies.speaker: water-keeper
replies.text: Even is not the same as fair. The rows need six to stay alive; at five, a bucket of field work dies and the crew loses the whole round. A split that looks fair can waste water both sides needed.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on a reserve in the lower channel

replies.speaker: water-keeper
replies.text: A reserve of two is care for the next bell: if the intake slips, someone still has water. The weir should never run at the edge.

replies.speaker: water-scribe
replies.text: A reserve kept below is water the rows do not get today, decided by the people closest to the channel. A reserve is a choice about who waits. The register should say whose fields paid for it.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on following the larger queue

replies.speaker: civic-clerk
replies.text: Sixteen people waited at Canal Walk, fifteen at North Steps. A rule that follows the count is a rule anyone can check. Nobody has to trust my judgement, only the tally.

replies.speaker: civic-operator
replies.text: Sixteen against fifteen, and North Steps gets nothing. The count only holds people who could reach a desk in the workday. A rule can be easy to check and still shut out the people the count never saw.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on a window in each district

replies.speaker: civic-operator
replies.text: One window each means every street is on the first schedule. Then the count decides the rest. Access first, numbers second.

replies.speaker: civic-clerk
replies.text: A reserved window is a judgement we made, not one the count made. Next year another district asks for one, and we have no rule to say no, only how we felt this time.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on two windows each

replies.speaker: civic-clerk
replies.text: Two and two is simple and the same for everyone. A rule people can predict is a rule people can plan around.

replies.speaker: civic-operator
replies.text: The same for everyone is not the same as fair to everyone. North Steps has a stair and no ramp, and two windows there serve fewer people than two windows on the flat. Equal shares of a service are not equal access to it.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the carriers' wording

replies.speaker: voices-steward
replies.text: The crews' words carry how they remember the walk. Put them beside a plain direction, and a newcomer learns the way and the people who made it.

replies.speaker: voices-clerk
replies.text: Two lines on one sign, and a carrier with full hands reads neither. A remembered walk is precious. It still belongs in the archive with its date, not on a sign people must act on in a hurry.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the short route guide

replies.speaker: voices-clerk
replies.text: A short line gets a carrier to the lamp. The full account stays in the archive, dated and signed, for anyone who wants it.

replies.speaker: voices-steward
replies.text: A short line in the archive's voice, and the crews' words disappear from the walk they made. In ten years, people will think the archive named the path.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the excerpt by the queue

replies.speaker: voices-steward
replies.text: People wait at the desk with nothing to do. An excerpt there meets them where they are, and some will come back to hear the whole account.

replies.speaker: voices-clerk
replies.text: An excerpt away from its record is a quote without its permission and its date. Read in a queue, it becomes the whole story for most people.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the excerpt at the reading slot

replies.speaker: voices-clerk
replies.text: At the slot, the excerpt sits with its record and its permission. Anyone who reads it can check where it came from.

replies.speaker: voices-steward
replies.text: And only the people who reach the slot will read it. A voice kept safely where few people go is safe, and mostly unheard.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on a rail comparison every shift

replies.speaker: council-reader
replies.text: Check the watch against the rail at the start of every shift, and nobody has to trust a seal they did not see made. Each crew knows for itself.

replies.speaker: council-keeper
replies.text: Every shift, someone stands at the rail before loading, and the carriers wait. A test that must be repeated by everyone, every time, stops being a test people share. Knowledge we cannot pass on is knowledge we keep relearning.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the dated repair record

replies.speaker: council-keeper
replies.text: A dated seal lets one crew rely on a test another crew carried out, as long as it says when it runs out. That is how most knowledge works: we trust a check we did not make, with its limits written on it.

replies.speaker: council-reader
replies.text: A seal is only as good as the people who read the date. By the third shift, nobody looks. A watch that only agrees with its own record is the problem this hall was built to fix.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the ridge cart

replies.speaker: island-planner
replies.text: The trial gave us a last arrival and a crossing count for the ridge. It is the route we measured, so it is the route we can plan on.

replies.speaker: island-dockhand
replies.text: We measured one dry trial with a fresh crew. A loaded cart on the ridge in the afternoon is a different route with the same name. A plan built on one run is a hope with numbers on it.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the ferry from the upper landing

replies.speaker: island-dockhand
replies.text: The ferry carries all eight crates at once, and my crew knows that water. When a route has worked for years, that is evidence too.

replies.speaker: island-planner
replies.text: Years of good crossings, and none of them with eight crates on a fair day. Experience is evidence for the conditions it came from. The trial is the only number we have for this load.

twoReplies.heading: Two views on the marsh path

replies.speaker: island-planner
replies.text: The first pair reaches the rail crew soonest by the marsh, so the rail crew can start. Getting work moving early buys time for every later problem.

replies.speaker: island-dockhand
replies.text: Soonest for the first pair. The marsh path was never in the trial. If it floods at the turn of the tide, the first pair arrives wet and late, and the plan has nothing to say about it.
